title: Arrays, Strings & Hash Maps: Revision Notes
summary: Night-before revision notes on arrays, dynamic arrays, strings, hash maps and hash sets: operation costs, plus the two pointers, sliding window, prefix sum and frequency counting patterns.

chapters.title: Arrays and Strings: The Mental Model
points: Array = contiguous memory, so index access arr[i] is O(1) via base address + i*size
Insert or delete in the middle is O(n) because elements shift; at the end it is O(1)
Dynamic array (list, ArrayList, vector) grows capacity by a constant factor when full (vector often 2x, ArrayList 1.5x, CPython list ~1.125x), so append is amortized O(1) though one resize is O(n)
Strings are immutable in Python, Java and JS: s += c in a loop is O(n^2), so build a list and join once
Search in an unsorted array is O(n); in a sorted array binary search is O(log n)

chapters.title: Hash Maps and Hash Sets: Internals and Costs
points: Hash map stores key to value; hash set stores keys only; both give average O(1) insert, lookup and delete
Mechanism: hash(key) mod bucket count picks a bucket; collisions are resolved by chaining or open addressing
Worst case is O(n) when many keys collide; resizing at a load factor (~0.7 to 0.75) keeps the average O(1)
Keys must be hashable and immutable: a Python list cannot be a key, a tuple can
Hash map vs array: map gives O(1) lookup by any key but uses more memory and has no sorted order

chapters.title: Frequency Counting and Lookup Patterns
points: Count occurrences in one pass: Counter(s) in Python, or counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1, giving O(n) time and O(k) space for k distinct keys
Two Sum: store seen[value] = index and check target - x before inserting x, giving O(n) instead of O(n^2)
Anagram check: compare two frequency maps, or a 26-slot count array for lowercase letters
Duplicate detection: add each item to a set and return true when it is already present
Group by key: map tuple(sorted(word)), ''.join(sorted(word)) or a 26-count tuple to a list of words (Group Anagrams)

chapters.title: Two Pointers and Prefix Sums
points: Opposite-end two pointers: l=0, r=n-1 on a sorted array, move l up when the sum is too small and r down when too large; O(n) time, O(1) space
Same-direction (slow/fast) pointers: in-place dedupe or remove-element by writing at slow and reading at fast
Prefix sum: pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i]; range sum(l..r) = pre[r+1] - pre[l] in O(1) after O(n) build
Subarray sum equals k: keep a map of prefix sum to count and add count[running - k] at each step; O(n)
Choose by problem: sorted pairs use two pointers, repeated range queries use prefix sums, unsorted pair lookup uses a hash map

chapters.title: Sliding Window and Common Mistakes
points: Fixed window of size k: add a[i], subtract a[i-k], and update the best value each step; O(n)
Variable window: expand r each step, shrink l while the window is invalid, and record the best length; each index enters and leaves once, so O(n)
Longest substring without repeats: keep a set or a map of last-seen index and move l past the duplicate
Sliding window needs a monotonic validity rule; with negative numbers in a sum-based window it breaks, so use prefix sums plus a hash map
Mistakes: off-by-one on r-l+1 and the prefix array length n+1, mutating a list while iterating it, and using a list for membership tests (O(n)) instead of a set (O(1))

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Arrays, Strings and Hash Maps
points: Array: access O(1), search O(n), insert or delete in the middle O(n), append amortized O(1)
Hash map or set: insert, lookup and delete average O(1), worst O(n); no ordering
String: immutable, concatenation in a loop is O(n^2), use join; sort is O(n log n)
Pattern picker: pairs in a sorted array use two pointers; contiguous subarray or substring uses sliding window; range sums use prefix sums; counts, seen and complements use a hash map
Templates: Counter(s); seen = {}; pre = [0]; l = 0 with for r in range(n); Interview Point: why is append amortized O(1), when does sliding window fail, why can a hash map degrade to O(n)
